1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist uses **For** to introduce the reason for the preceding exhortation. Use a connector that is natural in your language for introducing a reason. Alternate translation: [Because it is good to make music to our God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising him]

The terms **pleasant** and **suitable** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very pleasant]

2.note: The expression **the scattered of Israel** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is their enemies. Alternate translation: [the Israelites whom enemies scattered]

3.note: The psalmist is speaking of **healing** emotional distress and **binding up their wounds** as if people’s sadness were physical injuries. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [comforting those who are very sad and relieving their pain]

The psalmist is using **the broken of heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “people who have suffered emotional wounds.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are deeply grieving]

5.note: The psalmist places the adjective **Great** before the subject for emphasis. If it would be more natural in your language, you could use standard word order. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our Lord is great]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [abundantly powerful]

The psalmist is using an extreme statement to emphasize how great God’s understanding is. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [greater than anyone can measure] or [beyond anyone’s ability to assess]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he understands] or [how much he comprehends]

6.note: The psalmist uses the adjective **poor** as a noun to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives similarly. If not, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are humble] or [people who are poor]

The psalmist is speaking of God humiliating **the wicked** as if he were physically **bringing** them **down** **to the ground**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [humbling the wicked] or [making the wicked fail]

The psalmist uses the adjective **wicked** as a noun to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives similarly. If not, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked] or [people who do wicked things]

7.q: עֱנ֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה בְּ⁠תוֹדָ֑ה זַמְּר֖וּ לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֣י⁠נוּ בְ⁠כִנּֽוֹר
7.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Make music to Yahweh our God with grateful singing and the harp]

The psalmist uses the imperative form here as an exhortation to worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this exhortation in a way that is natural for your language. Alternate translation: [Let us sing to Yahweh and give him thanks]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [giving thanks] or [thankfully]

9.note: The expression **the sons of the raven** is an idiom that means young ravens. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an idiom from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the young ravens]

9.q: נוֹתֵ֣ן לִ⁠בְהֵמָ֣ה לַחְמָ֑⁠הּ לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י עֹ֝רֵ֗ב אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִקְרָֽאוּ
9.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He gives its food to the beast, and he gives food to the sons of the raven when they call]

10.q: לֹ֤א בִ⁠גְבוּרַ֣ת הַ⁠סּ֣וּס יֶחְפָּ֑ץ לֹֽא־בְ⁠שׁוֹקֵ֖י הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ יִרְצֶֽה
10.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [He does not value the strength of a horse or the physical ability of a person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in how strong a horse is]

Although the term **man** is masculine, the psalmist is using it in a generic sense to refer to any person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [the legs of a person]

The psalmist is using one part of the body, **the legs**, to represent physical ability in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person’s physical ability] or [how fast a person can run]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for him to keep his covenant promises] or [for him to show them kindness because of his covenant]

12.q: שַׁבְּחִ֣י יְ֭רוּשָׁלִַם אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה הַֽלְלִ֖י אֱלֹהַ֣יִ⁠ךְ צִיּֽוֹן
12.note: The psalmist uses the imperative form here as an exhortation to worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this exhortation in a way that is natural for your language. Alternate translation: [You people of Jerusalem should praise Yahweh]

12.q: שַׁבְּחִ֣י יְ֭רוּשָׁלִַם אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה הַֽלְלִ֖י אֱלֹהַ֣יִ⁠ךְ צִיּֽוֹן
12.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh, you people of Jerusalem]

The psalmist is speaking to the city of **Jerusalem**, also called **Zion**, as if it could hear, but he is really addressing the people of that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, people of Jerusalem; praise your God, people of Zion]

13.note: The psalmist uses **For** to introduce the reason for the preceding exhortation. Use a connector that is natural in your language for introducing a reason. Alternate translation: [Because he strengthens the bars of your gates]

14.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one making your borders safe and secure]

The psalmist is speaking of the best quality of **wheat** as if it were **the fat** part. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the finest wheat] or [with the best wheat]

15.note: The psalmist speaks of God’s **word** as if it were a person who could **run**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his word goes out very quickly] or [what he commands happens immediately]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **swiftness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [goes out very quickly]

16.note: The psalmist compares **snow** to **wool** to emphasize how the snow covers the ground in a white, soft layer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [snow that is white like wool]

The psalmist compares **frost** to **ashes** to emphasize how the frost is spread across the ground lightly and in fine particles. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [frost like gray ashes]

17.note: The psalmist compares **hail** to **crumbs** to emphasize that the hailstones are small pieces. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [his hailstones like small crumbs]

The psalmist uses a rhetorical question to emphasize that no one can endure God’s cold. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one can stand in such cold!] or [no one can endure when he makes it so cold.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cold**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his freezing weather] or [when he makes it freeze]

Here, **the face of** represents the presence or force of something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he sends his cold] or [outside in his freezing cold]

18.note: The psalmist is speaking of God’s **word** as if it were a messenger that God could **send**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gives a command, and he makes them melt]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe the **wind** that comes from God. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wind he sends]

19.note: The terms **statutes** and **judgments** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all his laws]

19.q: מַגִּ֣יד דבר⁠ו לְ⁠יַעֲקֹ֑ב חֻקָּ֥י⁠ו וּ֝⁠מִשְׁפָּטָ֗י⁠ו לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
19.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. A resulting parallelism is modeled in the UST. Alternate translation: [He declared his word to Jacob; indeed, he declared his statutes and judgments to Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **statutes**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the rules he has set]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the decisions he has judged]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent the descendants of Jacob, who was also called Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to Jacob’s descendants] or [to the people of Israel]
